entries.what_happened: One manuscript, 'A proof of Seymour's second-neighborhood conjecture' (OpenAI, dated 23 September 2026), claims Theorem 1.1: every nonempty finite oriented graph has a vertex v with |N₁⁺(v)| ≤ |N₂⁺(v)|, where N₂⁺(v) is the set of vertices at exact directed distance two from v (excluding v and its out-neighbours, each counted once). The proof is by contradiction. Proposition 2.1 reduces a minimal counterexample (fewest vertices, then fewest arcs) to a graph G with positive indegrees in which every nonempty proper vertex set U satisfies |U| + |F²(U)| < 2|F(U)|, where F is the one-step out-image; Lemma 2.2 (subset deficit, adapted from Seacrest's Lemma 4) and Lemma 2.3 (transitive-tournament blow-up) give this. Section 3 (Lemma 3.1, a pruning bound for two families of ordered pairs, proved by a rank/matching argument) and Proposition 4.1 then rule out any such G. The same manuscript also derives, in Section 5 (Corollary 5.1) via Seacrest's 2015 equivalences, vertex-weighted forms (for every nonnegative vertex weighting some v has η(N₁⁺(v)) ≤ η(N₂⁺(v)); and a total-mass-one weighting under which every v satisfies this) and an arc-weighted form, and in Section 6 (Corollary 6.1) directed-cycle consequences: a digraph with no directed triangle has some v with d⁺(v) ≤ |Z(v)| and n−1 ≥ 2d⁺(v)+d⁻(v); minimum in- and outdegree at least n/3 forces a directed triangle; and a regular digraph with d⁺ = d⁻ = r and directed girth 4 has n ≥ 3r+1.
entries.delivers: Claims to settle the problem as the list states it. The list asks whether every oriented graph (no loops, no parallel arcs, no digons) has a vertex with at least as many vertices at distance two as at distance one. Theorem 1.1 gives exactly that, for every nonempty finite oriented graph, with no connectivity, degree or order hypothesis; a sink satisfies it trivially. The manuscript measures out-distance; reversing all arcs gives the in-distance reading, so both readings are covered. Tournaments, the special case known as Dean's conjecture, are covered by the general statement. The manuscript's wording matches the list's: its abstract says it 'resolves Seymour's second neighborhood conjecture positively', and Section 1 calls Theorem 1.1 that resolution.
entries.remains: Nothing, if the claim is correct: the problem asks only for the existence of such a vertex in every oriented graph, which Theorem 1.1 states. The weighted forms and directed-cycle consequences (Sections 5 and 6) go beyond what the problem asks.
entries.conditional_on: None for Theorem 1.1 beyond published results it cites: Edmonds (1967) for the generic-rank/matching correspondence used in Lemma 3.1, and König's theorem (re-derived in the text). Corollary 5.1 (weighted and arc-weighted forms) rests on Seacrest (2015), Proposition 2 and Theorem 1, cited rather than proved in the manuscript; that dependence does not affect the problem's own statement.
entries.doubts: The argument is a long contradiction proof across Sections 2 to 4. Its most compressed step is the choice of coefficients in Lemma 3.1: the text relies on the cited Edmonds correspondence and a brief argument that the required minors can be nonzero at one real assignment (a product of nonzero polynomials). It does not flag this as sketched, but it is the least expanded part. The manuscript reports no computer verification. Its weighted and arc-weighted consequences depend on Seacrest's equivalences, which it cites and does not reprove.
